questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Joining the names an aria-labelledby list points at
questions.learningObjective: compute the accessible name a list of references produces
questions.stem: An empty button carries `aria-labelledby="sub main"`, and a helper computes its name with `el.getAttribute('aria-labelledby').split(' ').map(ref => textOf(ref)).join(' ').trim()`. Element `main` holds the text `Invoice 2026` and element `sub` holds the text `Billing`, and `sub` sits later in the document than `main`. What accessible name does the button end up with?

options.text: Billing Invoice 2026, because the texts are joined in the order the attribute lists the references
Invoice 2026 Billing, because the texts are joined in the order the elements sit on the page
options.misconception: believes the page's reading order decides how referenced texts are joined

options.text: No accessible name at all, because a control can only be named by the text inside itself
options.misconception: believes the element's own content is the only possible source of a name

options.text: Invoice 2026, because only the first element an attribute names can contribute to a name
options.misconception: believes a name stops being computed at the first referenced element

questions.explanation: The rule relied on is the order the attribute itself establishes: when a control is named by a list of references, the text of each referenced element is taken in the order the attribute lists them, joined with a space and trimmed, and that string is the name. Where the referenced elements happen to sit on the page is irrelevant, which is what makes it different from reading the page aloud. A referenced element need not even come before the control. The two traps are the natural one, joining in document order, and the assumption that a control can only be named by the content inside it, which is why an empty button with this attribute is named at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the attribute states an order or only names a set of elements.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Reading a tab order out of six focusable elements
questions.learningObjective: order the elements a sequence of Tab presses visits
questions.stem:
`document.querySelectorAll('a, button, input, [tabindex]')` returns six elements, and in document order they are: `Skip`, `
`, ``, `
`, `E`, ``. In what order does Tab visit them?

options.text: d, then b, then f, then skip, then c, and the link e is never visited
skip, then c, then d, then b, then f, and the link e is never visited
options.misconception: believes a positive tab index is applied after the elements that have none

options.text: skip, then c, then e, then d, then b, then f, so every element is reached
options.misconception: believes a negative tab index still leaves an element in the tab order

options.text: d, then b, then f, then skip, then c, then e, so a negative index comes last
options.misconception: believes a negative tab index queues an element at the end of the order

questions.explanation: The rule relied on is the definition of the focus navigation order: elements carrying a positive tab index come first, sorted by that value in ascending order, and every remaining focusable element follows in document order. A negative tab index takes an element out of that order while leaving it focusable by script, so e is skipped without becoming unfocusable. Note the consequence that surprises people: raising b and f above the skip link means a keyboard user meets page furniture before they are given the link that jumps past the furniture, which is why a positive index is usually the wrong tool for a skip link.
questions.hint: Decide which group comes first, then what a negative index does to an element.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a linearising contrast helper actually prints
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a contrast helper and account for each step in the ratio
questions.stem: This helper is meant to report the contrast between two hex colours: `const lin = (v) => Math.pow((v + 0.055) / 1.055, 2.4); const L = (hex) => 0.2126 * lin(parseInt(hex.slice(1,3),16)) + 0.7152 * lin(parseInt(hex.slice(3,5),16)) + 0.0722 * lin(parseInt(hex.slice(5,7),16)); const ratio = (a,b) => { const [x,y] = [L(a),L(b)].sort((m,n) => n - m); return (x + 0.05) / (y + 0.05); }; console.log(ratio('#767676', '#ffffff').toFixed(2));` What does it print?

options.text: 4.54, which is what the linearised channels and the weighting actually produce
2.05, which is the same ratio when the channels are left unlinearised
options.misconception: believes the channels can be used straight from the hex digits without being linearised

options.text: 2.16, which is the grey channel divided straight into the white one
options.misconception: believes contrast is the ratio of two raw channel values

options.text: 4.50, which is the value when the pair is taken to sit on the threshold
options.misconception: believes a passing pair of colours is written to land exactly on the limit

questions.explanation: The helper converts each channel to a value between 0 and 255, weights the three by the luminance coefficients, and then divides the brighter relative luminance plus 0.05 by the darker one plus 0.05. Running that on #767676 against #ffffff gives 4.54, which clears the 4.5 to 1 threshold for ordinary text by a small margin. The arithmetic is a formula to execute, not to estimate: leaving the channels unlinearised drops the answer to 2.05, and dividing 255 by 118 gives 2.16, both of which look plausible until you notice they are not measuring the quantity the threshold is written about. A colour that clears 4.5 usually clears it by a hair, not exactly.
questions.hint: Work the formula out loud: channel, weight, sum, then the plus 0.05 on each side.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Which controls survive into the tab order
questions.learningObjective: decide which of seven controls a keyboard user reaches
questions.stem:
One form contains ``, ``, `C`, `D`, `
E
`, `
F
` and ``, and a helper computes `controls.filter(c => !c.disabled && focusable(c))`. Which of the seven does Tab visit?

options.text: a, c, e and g, because a disabled control drops out and an anchor with no href was never focusable
a, b, c, e and g, because a disabled button is still visited so its state can be read
options.misconception: believes a disabled control stays in the tab order so that it is announced

options.text: a, b, d and e, because being read-only or disabled does not remove an element from the order
options.misconception: believes disabled and read-only are the same kind of state

options.text: all of them but d, because a negative tab index still leaves an element reachable by Tab
options.misconception: believes a negative tab index changes only where the element sits, not whether it is reached

questions.explanation: Three separate rules decide this. A disabled form control is removed from the tab order, which is why b is skipped and why a disabled control is announced as unavailable if a reader reaches it another way. An anchor is focusable only when it carries an href, so d was never in the order at all. A div with a non-negative tab index is focusable, which is what puts e in the order, and one with a negative value is focusable only by script, which is what keeps f out. A read-only input is still a perfectly ordinary field, so g is visited as usual.
questions.hint: Check each control against the three rules separately: disabled, natively focusable, tab index.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: How many announcements a sequence of live region writes produces
questions.learningObjective: count the live region updates a run of assignments produces
questions.stem:
A page loads with `

` already in the document, and a save handler then runs `el.textContent = 'Saving'; el.textContent = 'Saving'; el.textContent = 'Saved'; el.textContent = 'Saved'; el.textContent = 'Failed';` in that order. How many separate announcements does the reader hear?

options.text: Three, one for each time the region's text actually changes to a new value
Five, one for every assignment, because each write is an update to the region
options.misconception: believes any assignment to a live region counts as a change worth announcing

options.text: Two, because only the values that survive to the end of the handler are announced
options.misconception: believes intermediate values are replaced before anything is read out

options.text: One, because the reader waits for the handler to finish and then announces the final value
options.misconception: believes a live region reports only the value it settles on

questions.explanation: The rule relied on is that a live region is announced when its content changes, not when code writes to it. Assigning the value that is already there changes nothing, so the second and fourth writes are silent, and what remains is three announcements: Saving, Saved and Failed. This is also why writing a region once and then rewriting it with the same string is a common and completely silent bug. The other reading, that the reader waits for the handler to settle, describes a value in ordinary markup rather than a live region, and would mean a live region could never report progress.
questions.hint: Ask what makes an update worth announcing: the write, or the text that results.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The outline built from a heading sequence that skips a level
questions.learningObjective: build a heading outline and count the levels the page never wrote
questions.stem:
The headings on one page are `

Account

`, `

Profile

`, `

Contact

`, `

Billing

`, `

Cards

`, and a helper reads them with `headings.map(h => +h.tagName[1])`. How many entries does the navigable outline contain, and how many of them were implied rather than written?

options.text: Six entries, of which one is implied to hold the level between h2 and h4
Five entries, because a heading at a level nobody used is simply left out of the outline
options.misconception: believes a skipped level removes the heading from the outline instead of filling the gap

options.text: Seven entries, because every level between two headings is filled in twice over
options.misconception: believes the gap is filled at both ends rather than once in the middle

options.text: Six entries, all of them written by the page, because the gap is carried through unchanged
options.misconception: believes the outline is the raw list of heading levels with nothing inserted

questions.explanation: The outline is not the raw list of levels. The rule is that a heading which is more than one level deeper than the heading before it has an implied heading at each intermediate level, so an h2 followed by an h4 inserts an implied h3 and the outline becomes h1, h2, h3, h4, h2, h3: six entries, five of them written. Inserting the implied level is what keeps the tree navigable, because a user who steps into the h4 arrives at a h3 and can still step back out. The fix in the markup is to write the h3, not to remove the h4, and the heading's visual size is unrelated to any of this.
questions.hint: Ask what the level between h2 and h4 has to become for the tree to stay walkable.

questions.topic: Running an accessible name computation over a link holding an image
questions.learningObjective: compute a link's accessible name from the image inside it
questions.stem: A link contains only an image: ``. A helper is written as `const nameOf = (link) => (link.alt || link.title || link.textContent || '').trim();` and is called with the link, so `link.alt` is the image's alt value, `link.textContent` is empty and `link.title` is unset. What does it return?

options.text: Invoice 2026, because the first of the three sources that holds text wins
An empty string, because the name has to come from the link's own text content
options.misconception: believes text inside a descendant image cannot contribute to an ancestor's name

options.text: doc.png, because an image with no readable text falls back to its file name
options.misconception: believes the source address is used as the last name before giving up

options.text: An empty string, because the link holds no text of its own and no title is set
options.misconception: believes a name cannot be borrowed from anything nested inside the control

questions.explanation: The helper takes the first source that actually holds text, and in this case the image's alt value is that source, so it returns Invoice 2026. The rule behind it is that a control's accessible name is computed from its own contents, and the contents of a name-producing element nested inside the control count as the control's contents. A link that wraps nothing but an image is the standard case for this: the image is what carries the meaning, and the link borrows it. The empty answers all share one belief, that text must sit in the element being named, which is why so many icon links are reported as unnamed.
questions.hint: Ask which of the three sources is non-empty before worrying about which one is preferred.

questions.topic: What a skip link is for
questions.learningObjective: state the problem a skip link removes
questions.stem: The first focusable element on a page is a link reading `Skip to main content`, pointing at the id of the page's main region. What problem does having it first solve?

options.text: It lets a keyboard user get past the repeated navigation without tabbing through it on every page
It lets a screen reader user reload the page from the keyboard instead of finding the control
options.misconception: believes a link to an element in the page can refresh it

options.text: It stops the navigation links from being announced at all while the page is in use
options.misconception: believes naming a region hides the elements inside it from the reader

options.text: It makes the main region the first thing drawn on screen when the page opens
options.misconception: believes focus order and the painting order are the same thing

questions.explanation: On a page with a large site header, every page begins its tab order with the same run of navigation links, and a keyboard user pays for that run again on every page of the site. The skip link is the escape from it, and it only works if it is the first focusable thing in the document, which is why it is often hidden until it takes focus. It moves focus, so it helps keyboard users far more than it helps reader users, who can already jump by landmark. It has nothing to do with what is painted, and the element it points at must carry the id it names, or the link goes nowhere.
questions.hint: Think about what a keyboard user does on the second page as well as the first.

questions.topic: What marking a region as a landmark lets a user do
questions.learningObjective: say what a landmark region adds over an unmarked container
questions.stem: A page wraps its navigation links in a `nav` element. A screen reader user can move to that group of links as a unit. What does the element do that a `div` in the same place would not?

options.text: It exposes the region as a landmark, so the user can move to it by its type and its title
It has the links inside it skipped by default, because the region already names the group
options.misconception: believes a landmark removes its own contents from the reading order

options.text: It makes the region's title be spoken before the first link inside it is read
options.misconception: believes the element inserts a spoken heading at the start of the group

options.text: It stops the region's links from being counted as part of the page's own outline
options.misconception: believes a landmark is a heading that happens to contain links

questions.explanation: A landmark is a named region of the page, and its value is the list a reader keeps: the reader is holding the banner, the navigation, the main content, the complementary sidebar and the footer, and can jump to any of them without walking the document. The element supplies the type, and an accessible name on it, such as a label on the nav, is what lets a reader tell two navigation regions apart. None of that changes what is read inside the region: the links are still announced one by one when the user goes in, which is the whole reason the jump is worth having.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can do with the region that they could not do with a plain container.

questions.topic: Marking an image that carries no information
questions.learningObjective: mark a decorative image so it is passed over
questions.stem: An image is a hairline rule drawn between two sections, and it says nothing beyond that. How should it be marked so that it keeps its space and is not announced?

options.text: With an empty alt value, so it is passed over while the element still occupies its space
With alt text reading decorative divider, so the reason it is there is still available
options.misconception: believes a description of the decoration is more useful than passing over it

options.text: With no alt attribute at all, so the browser is free to choose the most helpful fallback
options.misconception: believes omitting the attribute lets the platform work out the right treatment

options.text: With the image left out of the markup and a border on the section, so there is nothing to read
options.misconception: believes the divider has to be removed before it can be ignored safely

questions.explanation: An empty alt value is the specific signal that an image is decorative: it tells assistive technology to skip the element while the element itself stays in the page and keeps its dimensions, which is what the border trick cannot do. A description of a divider is noise, because there is no information in it that the surrounding structure does not already carry. Omitting alt is the opposite of the signal, since a missing value is what sends readers off to fetch the file name or guess from context. The rule of thumb is that alt should say what the image adds, and here it adds nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the image contributes beyond the space it occupies.

questions.topic: What the role attribute changes and what it does not
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the reporting effect of a role from behaviour
questions.stem: A `div` carries `role="button"` and a key handler that calls the same function as its click handler. Which of the following has the role attribute actually changed?

options.text: What the element reports, so it is announced as a button instead of as unlabelled text
How the element behaves, so a click is dispatched on it without any listener being attached
options.misconception: believes naming a role installs the behaviour that the role implies

options.text: How the element responds to keys, so Enter and Space now activate it with no handler at all
options.misconception: believes a role brings key handling with it as well as the name and type

options.text: Where the element sits in the page's outline, so it counts as a heading of the same rank
options.misconception: believes any role puts an element into the document's heading structure

questions.explanation: A role is a declaration about semantics, so it changes what the element is reported as: its type, and with it the set of states and properties a reader knows it can have. It grants no behaviour of any kind, which is why the key handler is still required, and it grants no focus, which is why a div carrying this role still needs a non-negative tab index to be reachable at all. The confusion is reasonable because a real button element does come with all of that attached, and reading a role as a shorthand for a real element is the mistake that produces divs that are announced as buttons and do nothing when pressed.
questions.hint: Ask what a role describes and what it cannot possibly provide.

questions.topic: What aria-hidden takes out of the accessibility tree
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of marking a subtree as hidden
questions.practice: reviewing live region and hidden content
questions.stem: A small icon sits inside a link that already carries its own text, and the icon has `aria-hidden="true"`. What does that attribute do to the icon?

options.text: It removes the icon from the accessibility tree, so no reader ever announces it
It keeps the icon in the tree but announces it only when the link takes focus
options.misconception: believes hiding an element delays its announcement rather than removing it

options.text: It replaces the icon with the link's own text whenever the link is read out
options.misconception: believes a hidden element is substituted by its parent's accessible name

options.text: It announces the icon after the link's text, at a lower volume than the text itself
options.misconception: believes the attribute lowers the priority of an element rather than removing it

questions.explanation: The attribute removes the element and everything inside it from the accessibility tree, which is the structure a reader navigates, so its content is never announced and it contributes nothing to any name computed from its ancestors. That makes it the right tool for a duplicate of text that is already present, and for purely graphic decoration inside a control. The trap is reading hidden as softened: a reader does not speak it more quietly or later, it simply is not part of what the reader can reach, and the visible and the exposed trees are allowed to differ as a result.
questions.hint: Ask whether a hidden element is spoken differently or is not in the structure at all.

questions.topic: The contrast threshold for ordinary body text
questions.learningObjective: state the minimum contrast for normal text and how it is measured
questions.stem: Body text has to stay readable against whatever sits behind it. Applying the contrast requirement for ordinary text, what is the minimum ratio between the text colour and the background behind it?

options.text: 4.5 to 1, measured between the text colour and the colour behind it
3 to 1, which is the threshold that applies to text of every size on a page
options.misconception: believes the large-text threshold is the only one that exists

options.text: 7 to 1, which is the level every page is required to meet for any text
options.misconception: believes the strictest named level is the required minimum

options.text: 21 to 1, which is the ratio beyond which no two colours can be confused
options.misconception: believes the scale runs to pure black on pure white and that is the target

questions.explanation: Ordinary text needs 4.5 to 1. Larger text, meaning text at or above 24 pixels, or 18.66 pixels and bold, is allowed 3 to 1, which is why a heading and a caption drawn in the same grey can look fine together and fail for body copy. The ratio is computed from the relative luminance of the two colours, not from how the pair looks on a good monitor, and the two colours that matter are the text and whatever is actually behind that piece of text, which is sometimes an image rather than the page background. Measuring only against the page background is a common way to miss a failure.
questions.hint: Separate the threshold for ordinary text from the one that applies to large text.

questions.learningObjective: identify the change that gives table cells a header association

options.text: Use header cells for that row, so each data cell can be related to the column above it
Give every data cell a header attribute naming its column, so the name travels with the value

options.text: Add a caption naming the table, so the reader knows what the columns are before reading them
options.misconception: believes a caption replaces the per-cell association with the column name

options.misconception: believes each body cell needs its own header rather than one shared per column

options.text: The only cue telling a keyboard user which control they are on, on every control in the form
The ability to reach the buttons, because the outline is what made them focusable

options.text: The order in which the buttons are visited, because the outline also set the tab index
options.misconception: believes the focus indicator determines the sequence of focus movement

options.text: The name of each button, because the outline was drawn over the label text

questions.topic: Working out a contrast ratio and then counting the pairs that pass
questions.learningObjective: compute a contrast ratio and then apply the threshold across several pairs
questions.stem: Three greys are used as body text on a white page: #767676, #999999 and #595959. First give the contrast ratio for #767676 on #ffffff to two decimal places, then say how many of the three pairs reach 4.5 to 1.

options.text: 4.54, and two of the three
2.85, and two of the three
options.misconception: believes the ratio comes out at the value of the greyer of the two pairs without computing it

options.text: 4.54, and all three of them

questions.topic: Reading a tab order and then counting the presses needed

the skip link, the button, tabindex 1, tabindex 2, tabindex 3, in six presses

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a visible error message beside a field is not enough
questions.learningObjective: explain what an error message has to be connected to
questions.stem: Explain why putting a red error message directly under an input is not enough on its own, and what the message has to be connected to so that it arrives with the field.

answer.exemplar: A message placed under an input is a position, and a position is only information for someone who can see it. A reader moving through the form by field never goes there, so the field arrives with no indication that it is wrong and the correction is invisible. The message therefore has to be part of what the field reports: the field points at the message, so arriving at the field brings the message with it, and the field's own state is marked as invalid, so the reader knows the problem is attached to this control rather than being general news. Two further things follow. The message needs to say what to do, not merely that something is wrong, because a reader who cannot see which field is at fault cannot act on the diagnosis. And the summary at the top of the form, which is the right shape for a screen reader user who wants to know what to fix before working through twenty fields, has to link back to each field it names, or it stops the user having to hunt for the thing it is complaining about.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to name the problem as the difference between a visual position and a programmatic association, say that the field must point at its message and mark its own state, and note that the summary at the top needs to link to the fields it names. Merely saying that the message should be in the markup misses the mechanism, which is that a reader navigating by field does not visit the message at all.
questions.hint: Start by asking what a reader who arrives at the field learns from the message sitting below it.

options.text: The opening control records a reference to itself, so there is somewhere for focus to return
The dialog becomes visible and its contents are placed in the page
options.misconception: believes the dialog can be focused before its contents have been inserted

options.text: Focus is moved into the dialog, to its first interactive element or to the dialog itself
options.misconception: believes focus can be placed inside a dialog that is not yet in the page

options.text: A handler on the dialog keeps Tab and Shift+Tab within it while it stays open
options.misconception: believes the trap can be armed before focus is inside the dialog

options.text: On close, focus is moved back to the control recorded in the first step
options.misconception: believes focus returns to whatever happens to be first in the document

questions.explanation: Each step is forced by the one before it. The reference has to be taken while the opening control still has focus, because once the dialog is open the user is elsewhere and the element that opened it is the only sensible destination. The contents must be in the page before focus can be moved into them, since focus can only land on something that exists. The trap is armed after focus is inside, because a trap that holds nothing either lets the user out or drops focus on the document behind. The return comes last, and getting it wrong is what leaves focus at the top of the page after a dialog closes, which sends a keyboard user back through the whole header.
questions.hint: Ask what each step needs to have been true before it can run.

A form holds ``, `

phone, because one id may only be referenced once anywhere on a page

options.misconception: believes a control may hold only one reference in a description attribute

options.text: postcode, because a reference to a paragraph is dropped, and email gets one
options.misconception: believes only certain kinds of element can be described by a field

questions.stem: A browser fills a field only when the last token in its `autocomplete` value is one of the field names the platform defines, so a check like `tokens.filter(t => KNOWN.has(t)).length` counts the recognised ones. A checkout uses `name`, `email`, `postal`, `cc-number`, `one-time-code` and `favorite-color`. How many of the six are recognised?

Six, because any descriptive word may be used as an autofill field name
options.misconception: believes the browser accepts any sensible word as a field name

options.text: Three, because one-time-code is only honoured on a field inside a form element
options.misconception: believes a token is refused unless the field is inside a form

options.text: Two, because only the tokens the site's own login form uses are ever honoured
options.misconception: believes a browser only knows the field names one site has used

The important part is what happens next: an unrecognised token is ignored, with no error anywhere, so the field simply does not fill and the developer sees a field that is not working for a reason that never appears in a message. The autocomplete attribute is a hint about a value, not a label, and a hint the platform cannot use is the same as no hint at all.
questions.hint: Compare each token against the defined names, and count the ones that are not there.

questions.topic: Where focus lands after repeated presses inside a trap
questions.learningObjective: trace focus movement inside a modal dialog's trap
questions.stem: A dialog holds three focusable elements in document order: close, email, save. Focus starts on email, so `index` is 1. The key handler calls `e.preventDefault()` and then `index = (index + (e.shiftKey ? -1 : 1) + list.length) % list.length`, and moves focus to `list[index]`. Where is focus after four plain Tab presses?

options.text: On save, because the sequence from email runs save, close, email, save
On email, because four presses are two whole cycles of a three element list
options.misconception: believes the count of presses can be worked out from whole cycles only

options.text: On close, because the wrapping calculation starts from the top of the list
options.misconception: believes the calculation restarts at the first element each time

options.text: On the page behind the dialog, because a trapped key press never reaches the document
options.misconception: believes preventDefault stops the focus movement from happening

questions.explanation: From index 1, one press goes to 2, which is save, two goes to 0, which is close, three returns to 1, which is email, and four reaches 2 again, which is save. The wrapping is what makes it a trap: the modulo keeps every press inside the list, so a keyboard user can never reach the page behind the dialog by pressing Tab. That is the intended behaviour for a dialog and a serious failure in a panel that is not one, and the difference is whether there is a way out that does not depend on the trap, which for a dialog means the close control and the escape key.

questions.stem: A div with `role="button"` is wired as `el.addEventListener('keydown', e => { if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') { e.preventDefault(); activate(); } })` and `el.addEventListener('click', activate)`. A user produces five events in order: keydown Enter, keydown a, click, keydown space, keydown Tab. How many times does activate run?

options.text: Three times, once for Enter, once for the click and once for the space bar
Four times, because a key press whose default is prevented also activates
options.misconception: believes stopping the default action is itself a second activation

options.text: Two times, because the space bar is reserved for scrolling the page
options.misconception: believes a space bar press never activates a control

options.text: Five times, because the handler runs once for every event of any kind it sees
options.misconception: believes every event delivered to the element counts as an activation

questions.explanation: Two of the five events do nothing: the letter a is neither key the handler tests for, and Tab is navigation that a button is not expected to answer. Enter passes the test and activates, the click reaches the click listener and activates again, and the space bar passes the test too, which is the one beginners leave out, because a native button activates on the space bar and a custom control has to be told to. Preventing the default on the space bar is also what stops the page scrolling under the user, so that line is doing two jobs. Three activations, one per deliberate action.

questions.topic: The area a small padded control actually occupies
questions.learningObjective: compute the reach of a padded control and compare it with the minimum
questions.practice: tracing box sizing for touch targets
questions.stem: A stylesheet sets `.chip { display: inline-block; width: 20px; height: 20px; padding: 2px; border: 0; }` and nothing overrides the sizing rule, so the default one applies. What area can a pointer reach on this control, and does it meet the 24 by 24 CSS pixel minimum?

options.text: 24 by 24 pixels, because padding is added to the declared size under the default rule
20 by 20 pixels, because only the declared width and height can be reached by a pointer
options.misconception: believes padding is drawn but cannot be pressed

options.text: 28 by 28 pixels, because the default rule adds the padding on both sides twice over
options.misconception: believes the padding is counted once per side and then again in full

options.text: 20 by 20 pixels, which is allowed because the surrounding spacing is wide enough
options.misconception: believes generous spacing excuses a target that is smaller than the minimum

questions.explanation: Under the default sizing rule the declared width and height are the content box, so the box a pointer can reach is the content plus the padding on each side: 20 plus 2 plus 2, which is 24 by 24 and clears the minimum exactly. This is where small icon buttons usually fail, because a 20 by 20 icon drawn inside a 44 by 44 button is fine while the same icon alone is not, and a border of zero here means there is nothing else being added. The spacing exception is real but it is a separate argument about the neighbourhood, and relying on it is how a control ends up too small the moment someone removes a neighbouring element.
questions.hint: The default rule makes the declared size the content box, so add the padding on each side.

questions.topic: Clipping caused by a text spacing override
questions.learningObjective: compute whether text still fits after the spacing override
questions.stem: A paragraph sits inside a box of `height: 120px; overflow: hidden` and is set to `font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.2`, where it renders as six lines. A reader applies the text spacing override, which sets the line height to 1.5 times the size and leaves the size of the text alone. Does the text still fit?

options.text: No, because six lines of 24 pixels need 144 pixels against a 120 pixel box
Yes, because the extra leading falls outside the box and the height stays near 115 pixels
options.misconception: believes added line spacing does not count towards the height of the text

options.text: Yes, because a box with a declared height grows to hold whatever is put inside it
options.misconception: believes a declared height follows the content instead of clipping it

options.text: No, because the override also scales the size of the text, so the block needs 192 pixels
options.misconception: believes the text spacing override scales the text along with the spacing

questions.explanation: At the authored line height the six lines take 6 times 16 times 1.2, which is 115.2 pixels and fits inside 120. Under the override each line becomes 16 times 1.5, which is 24 pixels, so the block needs 144 and is 24 pixels over, which is exactly the last line. The override is worth understanding precisely because it does not change the size of the text, only the space around it, and it is applied by a reader's own settings rather than by the page. A container with a fixed height and hidden overflow is the shape that fails here, and the fix is to let the container grow rather than to hope nobody raises their line spacing.

questions.topic: What a fixed page width costs a reader who zooms
questions.learningObjective: compute the room left for a fixed layout at high zoom
questions.stem: A page wrapper is `width: 960px` inside an otherwise fluid layout. On a window 1280 pixels wide, a reader zooms the page to 400 percent. How much room is left for the page in CSS pixels, and how much of the wrapper sits past the edge?

options.text: 320 pixels of room, with 640 pixels of the wrapper past the edge of the window
1280 pixels of room, with nothing past the edge, because zooming only scales the drawing
options.misconception: believes zooming enlarges the picture without reducing the room available

options.text: 640 pixels of room, with 320 pixels past the edge, because the window loses half its width
options.misconception: believes a quadrupling of zoom halves the width available to the page

options.text: 960 pixels of room, with the wrapper fitting as comfortably as it does at full size
options.misconception: believes a fixed width keeps its relationship to the window at any zoom

questions.explanation: Zoom in a desktop browser is not a magnification of a drawing; it is a larger CSS pixel, so the window's width expressed in CSS pixels falls as the zoom rises, and 1280 device pixels at 400 percent is 320 CSS pixels. That is the whole reason the reflow requirement is written as 320 CSS pixels, because it is what a 1280 pixel window becomes at 400 percent. A wrapper fixed at 960 pixels then has 640 pixels that can only be reached by scrolling sideways, which is exactly the loss the requirement exists to prevent. Fluid widths and no fixed maximum on the body are what make the same page work at that size.
questions.hint: Convert the window width to CSS pixels by dividing by the zoom, then subtract from the fixed width.

questions.topic: Why a table used for layout misleads
questions.learningObjective: state what a layout table reports and why that is wrong
questions.stem: A two column layout is built from a table whose cells hold a photo and a caption, and a screen reader announces 'table, one row, two columns' before the photo. What is wrong with that announcement?

options.text: It describes a grid of related cells that the page does not have, so the reader is misled
It is read out before the contents, so the photo is announced later than the caption
options.misconception: believes the announcement delays the contents that follow it

options.text: It cannot be produced without a stylesheet, since tables only lay out when styled
options.misconception: believes a table only becomes a layout once it has been styled

options.text: It names the row and column counts, which forces the reader to navigate the cells
options.misconception: believes announcing the shape obliges the reader to move through the cells

questions.explanation: A table element reports itself as a table, and the shape it reports is the shape the reader then expects to navigate: a grid whose cells relate to one another, which a reader can use to compare a row or a column. In a layout table those relationships are not there, so the announcement is a promise the page does not keep, and reading every cell of a layout table is a well known way to lose a reader. The fix is either to stop using a table for layout, or to take the table role off it, and neither fix should cost the visual layout the page was built around.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader is told to expect, and whether the page is that shape.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a trap from a dialog that holds focus
questions.stem: Focus moves into a panel, and neither Tab nor Shift+Tab can move it out again. The only exit is a key the panel handles itself. What makes that a keyboard trap rather than a dialog doing its job?

options.text: There is no route out at all, so a keyboard user who cannot find the exit is stranded
Focus sits inside the panel while the panel is open, which is what every dialog does
options.misconception: believes holding focus is the definition of a trap

options.text: The panel is drawn over the page, so the controls underneath cannot be seen
options.misconception: believes covering the page is what prevents the keyboard reaching it

options.text: The panel can be opened without being asked for, so focus arrives unexpectedly
options.misconception: believes the surprise of the focus move is what makes it a trap

The failure is the absence of an exit: a trap is focus that cannot be moved out of by any key the user would think to press, and the only way out is something they have to discover. questions.learningObjective: identify a meaning carried by colour alone and the signal that is missing
questions.stem: A form marks its required fields with a red border and marks a field that failed validation with the same red border, and there is no other difference. Which statement describes what that encoding costs?

Anyone on a slow connection, because the styles arrive after the fields are shown
options.misconception: believes a late stylesheet is the reason a colour carries meaning

options.text: Anyone on a small screen, because a border is too thin to see on a phone
options.misconception: believes the size of a border decides whether a colour can carry meaning

options.text: Anyone using a reader, because a border colour is never announced at all
options.misconception: believes a colour is spoken out by readers and is the problem

Only the last line is announced, because the earlier ones are replaced before they are read
options.misconception: believes a region reports its final content and discards the rest

options.misconception: believes a region only reports transitions from empty to filled

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a challenge that only some people can pass excludes the rest
questions.learningObjective: explain the objection to a challenge and what should replace it
questions.stem: Explain the accessibility objection to a challenge that asks a person to identify objects in pictures, and say what should take its place when abuse is the concern it is meant to stop.

answer.exemplar: The task is defined by a perceptual ability rather than by an action, so the barrier lands on a group rather than on a behaviour. A person using a screen reader cannot be shown a picture of traffic lights and asked to select them, a person with a low vision impairment may not be able to resolve the small distorted images at all, and a person with a motor impairment may be unable to trace the target accurately enough to click it. The cost is also a poor exchange: the challenge makes the sign-up form longer for everyone and it excludes a real minority of people outright, so what it buys is a modest reduction in automated submissions. The abuse it targets comes from a specific behaviour, and behaviours are cheaper to stop than abilities are to test. A rate limit, a proof of work challenge, an email that must be confirmed, or a delay before an account can post are all things a person of any ability can complete, and they put the cost on the script rather than on the reader. If a human judgement is genuinely needed, it should be reserved for the few cases that reach it, and never be the only way in.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to name the objection as a barrier defined by perceptual ability rather than by behaviour, say which users it excludes, and then propose a replacement that puts the cost on the automated caller rather than on the person. Merely saying that the challenge is inconvenient misses the point, which is that it is a test a reader cannot pass however carefully they try.
questions.hint: Ask what the challenge measures, and who cannot do the measuring, before asking what it prevents.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: A page described as accessible and what a keyboard walkthrough shows
questions.learningObjective: explain how a keyboard walkthrough can contradict a claim about a page
questions.stem: A colleague reports that a page has been made accessible, and you are asked to confirm it. Explain what a keyboard walkthrough of that page would show, and why its verdict can contradict the report.

answer.exemplar: The walkthrough is a specific, repeatable thing rather than an opinion, and it tests the claims that matter most. Put the mouse away, open the page, and press Tab from the top: does the first stop skip the header, is there a visible indicator on every control you reach, can you leave whatever you land in, does the order follow the reading order, and does every control have a name you can hear. Then activate each one with both the keyboard and a pointer and compare. Each of those steps is a claim somebody can make about the page, and each is answered by observation rather than by reading the markup. This is why the walkthrough can contradict the report without either party being careless. Most accessibility work is done against the source, where a missing label is visible and a missing focus state is a rule that can be read, and a page can pass every check in the source and still fail on the page, because a rule can be present and produce nothing. A control can be focusable and be announced as a group of text, a name can be computed from content that is hidden, and a focus style can exist and be painted under a background. The report is also usually made by the person who did the work, describing intent, and the walkthrough describes behaviour, so the disagreement is usually about which of those is being reported.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to say that the walkthrough produces observations rather than opinions, list the specific things it would test, and explain the reason for the disagreement, which is that source review and behaviour are different questions and a page can pass the first and fail the second. Merely recommending a keyboard test misses the point, which is that it is the only way to find the failures that are present in the markup and produce nothing on the page.
questions.hint: List what pressing Tab actually checks, then ask why reading the source cannot answer the same questions.

Three, because every nav element is exposed regardless of what contains it

options.misconception: believes the containment test keeps the inner element and drops the outer one

That is why a site header's menu and the page's own secondary menu are two entries in a reader's landmark list, and why the two need distinguishable names if both are called navigation.

Nothing about headings, list grouping or scroll position is what decides where focus is, and each of those is a real thing to get right, just not this thing.
questions.hint: Ask where the next key press will be acted on, and whether that is what the user is looking at.

questions.topic: Autofill tokens written on the form instead of the fields
questions.learningObjective: identify where a field's autofill token has to be written
questions.stem: A checkout form carries `autocomplete="on"` on the form element and nothing on any of its inputs, and a tester reports that the browser never fills any of the fields. Which single change is the one that matters?

options.text: Write the field name for each purpose on the input itself, since that is where it is read
Add a stylesheet that makes the inputs read-only, so the browser offers its own values
options.misconception: believes making a field read-only is what makes autofill possible

options.text: Move the autocomplete attribute onto the body element, so the whole page is covered
options.misconception: believes the attribute works as a page-wide declaration

options.text: Replace the inputs with text controls that have no name, so no stale value can conflict
options.misconception: believes removing the field's name is what lets the browser fill it

questions.explanation: The token is read from the control the value belongs to, and on a form element it is a single setting for the whole form rather than a description of any one field, so it tells the platform that fields may be autofilled and nothing about what they are. The value on each input has to name a purpose from the defined vocabulary, and an unrecognised word is passed over without complaint, which is why the failure is always silent. The other three changes are unrelated to how autofill is discovered: read-only, where the attribute sits, and the presence of a name attribute have no bearing on it.
questions.hint: Ask which element the token has to be written on for it to describe a field's purpose.

Six regions, of which three are navigation landmarks

options.text: Five regions, of which one is a navigation landmark
options.misconception: believes a nav inside a header is absorbed into the banner and not listed

options.text: Three regions, of which two are navigation landmarks
options.misconception: believes the header and the footer are not regions of their own

Two of the five are navigation, which means a reader's landmark list names the page's navigation three times over unless the regions are given names that tell them apart, and that naming is the part that actually makes the list usable.

questions.topic: Reading a contrast ratio against the large text threshold
questions.learningObjective: compute a ratio and then judge it against the large-text threshold
questions.stem: Body text and headings are both drawn in #999999 on a white page, and the headings are 24 pixels. First give the contrast ratio for #999999 on #ffffff to two decimal places, then say whether the heading colour reaches the 3 to 1 that large text is allowed.

options.text: 2.85, and it does not reach 3 to 1, so the heading fails as well
4.54, and it clears 3 to 1, so the heading passes even though the body fails
options.misconception: believes a ratio from a different grey is the one that applies here

options.text: 2.85, and it clears 3 to 1, because the threshold is a comparison with the body text
options.misconception: believes large text is measured against the body colour rather than the background

options.text: 3.00, and it exactly reaches 3 to 1, so the heading is allowed
options.misconception: believes a designer will pick a grey that lands exactly on the threshold

questions.explanation: The relative luminance of #999999 against white gives 2.85, and 2.85 is below 3, so the heading fails the relaxed threshold that its size earns it. This is the item worth building a habit around, because the size allowance is often treated as a way of rescuing a colour: it does relax the requirement from 4.5 to 3, and a grey that passes at 4.5 is comfortably fine at 24 pixels, but a colour that was already too light is not rescued by making the text bigger. Both numbers come from the same formula, and the threshold a given piece of text must clear is set by its own size rather than by the size of the text next to it.
questions.hint: Compute the ratio first, then compare that one number with 3, not with the body threshold.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a widget must provide once it stops being a real control
questions.learningObjective: explain what replacing a native control takes on
questions.stem: Explain what a team takes on when it replaces a real select or button with a div, and why the saving is smaller than it looks.

answer.exemplar: A real control arrives with a contract attached, and most of what it costs is the contract. It is focusable and reports that it is focusable, it is in the tab order in the right place, it has a role, and it has whatever states apply to it. It can be operated with a pointer, with a key, and with whatever assistive technology the reader is using, including the screen reader commands that assume a button is a button. It behaves the way the platform's own style expects, and it works in the browser's own forms, which matters for a reader who never sees the styled version at all. Replace it with a div and each of those becomes a thing to write: a role, a tab index, a key handler that answers the keys the real control answered, a state that has to be exposed and kept current, a value that still has to reach the form, and a name. The one thing that is genuinely easier to control is the appearance, and that is the part a team usually wants. The saving is therefore real but small, and the cost lands on the people who did not write it, in a component that passes every review because the styling is right and fails the first person who tries to use it from the keyboard.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to enumerate what a real element supplies, name the four obligations that move to the team, and conclude that the styling is the only part that genuinely gets easier. Merely saying that custom controls are more work misses the mechanism, which is that the native element is carrying a contract the replacement has to reimplement.
questions.hint: List what the platform gives a real element before describing what the replacement must do.

questions.topic: The order a failed submission is handled in
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that make a failed submission usable
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order a page has to carry them out after a submission is rejected, from checking the values to telling the user what to fix.

options.text: The submitted values are checked, and the fields that failed are collected
A summary listing every failed field is built from what was collected
options.misconception: believes the summary can be written before the failures are known

options.text: The message for each failed field is placed next to that field and pointed at by it
options.misconception: believes field messages can be written before the summary that names them

options.text: Focus is moved to the summary, so the user is told what happened before they go looking
options.misconception: believes focus can be sent to a summary that has not been built yet

options.text: Each entry in the summary is a link that moves focus to the field it names
options.misconception: believes the links can be made before the summary exists to hold them

questions.explanation: Every step depends on the one before it. The check has to run before there is anything to report, the collection has to be complete before the summary is written, the field messages have to exist before a field can point at them, and the summary has to be in the page before focus can be sent to it. The links go last because they are what makes the summary worth arriving at: a summary that names three fields without letting the user reach them has told a reader how much work is ahead and nothing about how to start. This is the order to write down when a form's failure handling is being designed, because each omission shows up as a specific dead end.
questions.hint: Ask what each later step needs to have been produced by the earlier ones.

questions.topic: The order a native select is turned into a listbox
questions.learningObjective: sequence the work that turns a native control into a custom one
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order a team has to carry them out when it replaces a native select with a custom listbox.

options.text: The value the listbox is showing is kept, since the form and the page both depend on it
A role is given to the wrapper, so the element reports itself as a listbox
options.misconception: believes a listbox reports itself correctly with no role at all

options.text: The element is made focusable, so the keyboard can reach it at all
options.misconception: believes a wrapper can receive focus without being given a tab index

options.text: The key handler is written, so the arrow, home and end keys move the selection
options.misconception: believes a selection can be moved before the keys that move it are handled

options.text: The active option is exposed on the element, so a reader follows the selection
options.misconception: believes the active option can be exposed before a selection exists

questions.explanation: The order is set by what each piece needs to already exist. There has to be a value before anything can display or submit one, and it is the thing every later step reports against, which is why losing it is the most common way a custom select ends up decorative. The role comes next because it is what makes the element a listbox to a reader rather than a box of text, and focusability has to follow, since an element that is not focusable cannot receive the keys that come after. The key handler then has something to move, and only once a selection exists is there an active option to expose, which is what lets a reader follow it without the selection moving physically into the tree.
questions.hint: Ask what each piece of the widget needs to have been built before it can exist.

questions.topic: The order a new screen has to hand focus over
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that make a screen change perceivable
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order a single page application has to carry them out when a link replaces one screen with another.

options.text: The new screen is rendered in place of the old one
The document title is set to the new screen's name, so the page reports where it is
options.misconception: believes the title can be set before the screen it describes exists

options.text: Focus is moved to the heading that starts the new screen, so the user is placed in it
options.misconception: believes focus can be sent into a screen that has not been rendered

options.text: The announcement naming the new screen is made, once the user is known to be in it
options.misconception: believes the announcement has to come before the user is moved

options.text: The tab position is reset to the top of the new screen rather than kept from the old one
options.misconception: believes the previous screen's tab position should carry over to the new one

questions.explanation: Nothing can report a screen that has not been rendered, so the render comes first, and the title follows it because the title is one of the things that describes the new screen rather than causing it. Focus then moves to the heading that opens the new content, which is what stops the user's next key press from landing on a control from the screen they have just left, and the announcement follows the move, because there is no point telling a reader where they are before they are there. The tab position is reset last, and it is the step that decides whether Tab on the new screen starts at its beginning or somewhere in the middle.
questions.hint: Ask which of these steps needs something to already be on the page before it can run.
